603.title: Entertaining angels (Hebrews 13:1–2)
603.howItsDone: Catholic parishes, religious houses and charities practice hospitality to strangers, from welcoming newcomers at Mass to meals and shelter for travelers and the homeless, and Benedictine monasteries still receive guests as Christ, following the Rule of Saint Benedict.

segments.voice: Yesterday, faith: the substance of things hoped for, and a family list that isn't closed. Your line was faith is the substance.

The hottest part of the day. An old man sits at the door of his tent, under the oaks of Mamre, and looks up to see three strangers standing nearby. He doesn't wait to find out who they are. He runs to meet them, bows to the ground, and has bread baked and a calf prepared while they rest in the shade. That's Abraham in Genesis eighteen, and by the end of the visit it's clear these were no ordinary travelers. Centuries later, in the last chapter of Hebrews, among a few short pieces of advice, the writer reaches back for that afternoon.
screen: `THREE STRANGERS AT MAMRE.` → `ABRAHAM RUNS TO MEET THEM.` → `HEBREWS REMEMBERS THAT AFTERNOON.`

segments.voice: Chapter thirteen puts two kinds of love side by side: love for the family of believers, and love for people you don't know at all. The Douay-Rheims puts it this way: "And hospitality do not forget; for by this some, being not aware of it, have entertained angels." The King James Bible ends the verse with the phrase in today's line: angels unawares. The Greek word behind hospitality is philoxenia, simply love of strangers. Not love of guests you invited; love of the person you didn't expect. Hebrews names no one here, but readers often think of stories like these. Abraham at Mamre, feeding three visitors. Lot, taking two strangers into his house in Sodom. And Catholic Bibles hold another, in the book of Tobias: a young man sets out on a long journey with a hired companion who calls himself Azarias, and only at the very end does the companion reveal that he is the angel Raphael. A whole road trip, and nobody knew. Notice what Hebrews doesn't say. It doesn't promise that every stranger is an angel, or tell you to be kind in case one is. The point runs the other way: you can't sort people in advance, so welcome everyone. Jesus says it even more directly in Matthew twenty-five: "I was a stranger, and you took me in." Saint Benedict wrote it into his rule for monks: every guest who comes to the door is to be received as Christ himself.

If you pray, hold the line I was a stranger, and you took me in; if not, just hold the face kindly.

604.title: Every best gift (James 1:17)
604.hook: every good gift comes from the Father of lights
604.howItsDone: Catholics give thanks for God's gifts in grace before meals, in the thanksgiving after Communion, and in the Mass itself, whose name Eucharist comes from the Greek for thanksgiving.

segments.voice: Yesterday, angels unawares: philoxenia, love of the stranger you didn't expect. Your line was angels unawares.

A sundial works only because the light keeps moving. Morning shadows stretch long to the west, shrink to almost nothing at noon, and swing around to the east by evening. The sun is faithful, but it never holds still, and everything it touches casts a shadow that turns. Winter days are short, summer days are long, clouds come and go. In the first chapter of a new letter, the letter of James, James looks up at that moving sky and says something about the one who made it.
screen: `A SUNDIAL NEEDS MOVING LIGHT.` → `EVERY SHADOW TURNS.` → `A NEW LETTER: JAMES.`

segments.voice: The letter opens simply: James, the servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ, to the twelve tribes scattered abroad. Which James? The letter doesn't say. Early tradition named James of Jerusalem, called the brother of the Lord, and Catholic tradition has often identified him with James the Less, one of the twelve. Scholars still discuss it. Then, almost at once, James talks about trials and temptation, and draws a firm line. When someone is tempted, they shouldn't say God is tempting them. God tempts no one. Temptation grows from a person's own desires. So where does God come in? Here, in the Douay-Rheims: "Every best gift, and every perfect gift, is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom there is no change, nor shadow of alteration." Some readers hear the lights of Genesis one here: the sun, the moon, the stars, which God made. Those lights move. They wax and wane, rise and set, and the shadows they cast turn all day long. God doesn't. With him, James says, there's no shadow of alteration. The good he gives isn't a passing mood that will swing around by evening. And the very next verse names one gift in particular: of his own will God has brought us to birth by the word of truth. Put it together and the line becomes a habit of attention. The good things in a life, the friend, the meal, the recovery, the morning, have a source, and James traces them up.

605.title: Doers of the word (James 1:19–27)
605.hook: swift to hear, slow to speak, and not hearers only
605.howItsDone: At every Mass Catholics hear readings from scripture and a homily, and the Mass ends with a dismissal sending the people out; many parishes link the Sunday word to works of mercy such as visiting the sick, the elderly and the bereaved.

segments.voice: Yesterday, every best gift: from the Father of lights, with whom there is no change. Your line was from above.

On your way out the door you catch yourself in the hall mirror. Hair sticking up. Something green in your teeth. You see it clearly; you even make a face at it. Then your keys are in your hand, the door shuts behind you, and by the time you reach the car the mirror is gone from your mind, and so is the spinach. Two hours later someone at work tells you. James uses a moment like it, a man and a mirror, to describe the way people listen to God's word.
screen: `THE HALL MIRROR ON THE WAY OUT.` → `YOU SAW IT, THEN FORGOT.` → `JAMES HAS A MIRROR TOO.`

segments.voice: It starts with three speeds. The Douay-Rheims: "let every man be swift to hear, but slow to speak, and slow to anger." Fast ears, slow mouth, slower temper. A quarrel runs the other way round. Then the line this passage turns on: "But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves." Hearing can feel like progress. A good homily, a moving reading, a podcast that lands, and it's easy to think, there, that's done. James says that feeling can fool you. Here comes the mirror. Someone who hears the word and doesn't do it is like a man who looks at his own face in a glass, walks away, and forgets at once what he looked like. The word shows you yourself; the question is whether you do anything about what you saw. The Greek for doers is poietai, makers. Greek used the same word for a poet. So a doer of the word makes something out of what they heard. Then James gets practical. Rein in your tongue. And he gives a short definition of religion that's hard to wriggle out of: religion that's pure in God's sight is this, "to visit the fatherless and widows in their tribulation," and to keep yourself unstained by the world. Not more listening. Visiting. Catholics hear the word at every Mass, and at the end the people are sent out: go. The hearing happens inside. The doing happens on the way home.
screen: `SWIFT TO HEAR, SLOW TO SPEAK.` · `HEARING CAN FOOL YOU.` · `THE MAN AT THE MIRROR FORGETS.` · `VISIT THE FATHERLESS AND WIDOWS.` · then, large: `BE YE DOERS OF THE WORD.`

segments.voice: Let one phrase come back from the last Mass you went to, or any line of scripture from this week; take the first that sticks, not the best. If you pray, ask for help to do it; if not, just choose it and hold it.

606.title: Faith without works (James 2:14–26)
606.hook: faith without works is dead; Catholics hold Paul and James together, and Christians have long discussed them
606.howItsDone: The Catholic Church teaches that justification is a free gift of grace received in faith, and that faith comes alive in charity; Catholics express this through the corporal and spiritual works of mercy, such as feeding the hungry, clothing the naked and visiting the sick.

segments.voice: Yesterday, poietai: makers, not the man who sees his face in the mirror and forgets. Your line was doers, not hearers.

It's cold out. A man with no coat stops you on the sidewalk and says he hasn't eaten since yesterday. Say you smile, look him in the eye, and tell him warmly: go in peace, stay warm, eat well. Then you walk on, meaning every word, maybe planning to pray for him later. James sets up exactly this scene in his second chapter, and asks one blunt question: what good is that? Christians have talked about what that question means ever since.
screen: `A MAN WITH NO COAT.` → `GO IN PEACE, STAY WARM.` → `WHAT GOOD IS THAT?`

segments.voice: James's answer is famous. In the Douay-Rheims: "For even as the body without the spirit is dead; so also faith without works is dead." Faith that never moves is like a body with no breath in it. Then he pushes further. You believe there is one God? Good. "The devils also believe and tremble." Knowing the right things isn't the same as trusting God with your life. He points to Abraham offering Isaac, and to Rahab, who hid the spies: their faith showed itself in what they did. Now the puzzle. Paul, writing to the Romans, says we are justified by faith, without the works of the law. James says, "Do you see that by works a man is justified; and not by faith only?" Are they arguing? Christians have discussed this for centuries, and they don't all answer the same way. Catholic teaching holds the two together. Salvation is a free gift of grace that nobody can earn; Paul is clear about that. And the faith that receives it is meant to come alive in love; James is clear about that. Paul himself puts both in one phrase in Galatians: "faith that worketh by charity." A common Protestant reading puts it this way: we are saved by faith alone, and living faith always produces good works, which is what James is describing. In nineteen ninety-nine, the Catholic Church and the Lutheran World Federation signed a joint declaration saying they share a basic understanding of justification, while naming the differences that remain. On a Tuesday, though, James's test is simple. Look at the man with no coat. Faith shows up as a coat.

If you pray, offer them both to God.

607.title: Is any man sick (James 5:13–16)
607.hook: call the priests to anoint the sick: the Church's root for anointing
607.howItsDone: In the sacrament of the Anointing of the Sick, a priest prays over a seriously ill or elderly person, lays hands on them in silence and anoints their forehead and hands with oil blessed by the bishop; families can ask their parish or a hospital chaplain for it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, faith without works: a body with no breath. Your line was faith that works.

Many parish priests carry a small metal case, about the size of a lipstick, with a screw-top lid. Inside is a bit of cotton soaked in olive oil, blessed by the bishop during Holy Week. It rides in a coat pocket or a glove box for months. Then one night the phone rings: a hospital, a nursing home, a kitchen where someone's father has taken a turn. The priest drives over, takes out the little case, and does something Christians have done since the first century. The instructions come from the end of the letter of James.
screen: `A SMALL METAL CASE OF OIL.` → `THE PHONE RINGS AT NIGHT.` → `INSTRUCTIONS FROM JAMES.`

segments.voice: James ends with three quick questions. Is anyone sad? Let him pray. Is anyone cheerful? Let him sing. And then, in the Douay-Rheims: "Is any man sick among you? Let him bring in the priests of the church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord." Notice who moves first. The sick person calls. Nobody is meant to suffer quietly in a back room so as not to be a bother. James goes on: "And the prayer of faith shall save the sick man: and the Lord shall raise him up: and if he be in sins, they shall be forgiven him." The Greek word for those priests is presbyteroi, elders, and the English word priest grows out of it. The Church sees here the root of a sacrament, the Anointing of the Sick. The Council of Trent taught that it was hinted at in Mark's Gospel, where the twelve anointed many sick people with oil, and made known by James. For centuries it was mostly given at the very end of life and called Extreme Unction, the last anointing. After the Second Vatican Council the Church stressed its older name and wider use: anyone seriously ill, someone facing major surgery, the frail elderly, and it can be received more than once. The priest lays his hands on the person in silence, then anoints the forehead and the hands. The Church doesn't promise a cure. It speaks of strength, peace and courage, and of bodily healing too, if God wills it. Saved and raised up can mean more than one thing.

608.title: A living hope (1 Peter 1:3–9)
608.hook: born again into a living hope through the resurrection
608.howItsDone: Readings from the first letter of Peter are heard at Mass during the Easter season, and Catholics count hope as one of the three theological virtues, with faith and charity, anchored in the resurrection of Christ.

segments.voice: Yesterday, presbyteroi: the elders called to pray over the sick and anoint them with oil. Your line was the prayer of faith.

In Luke's Gospel, Peter warms himself at a fire in a courtyard and says, three times, that he doesn't know Jesus. Then a rooster crows, and he goes out and weeps. Years later the same man, now a leader of the Church, writes to Christians scattered across what is now Turkey, people being mocked and pushed to the edges for their faith. He could open with a warning, a plan, a word about his own failures. Instead, after a short greeting, the first thing out of his pen is a blessing, and the blessing is about hope.
screen: `PETER BY THE COURTYARD FIRE.` → `YEARS LATER, A LETTER.` → `IT OPENS WITH HOPE.`

segments.voice: Here it is in the Douay-Rheims: "Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who according to his great mercy hath regenerated us unto a lively hope, by the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead." Lively: in older English, that meant living. The Greek says it plainly, a living hope. Not a wish. Not optimism, which is a weather forecast about how things will probably turn out. Peter's hope is anchored in something that already happened: a tomb that was empty, a friend he saw alive again. And he had his own reason to need it. On Easter morning, in Mark's Gospel, the message for the disciples names him in particular: go, tell his disciples and Peter. Then Peter describes what the hope looks toward, an inheritance with three nots. It can't perish. It can't be stained. It can't fade. In Greek all three begin with the same little a-, meaning not. Peter doesn't pretend the present is easy. His readers are grieving in various trials for a while, and he compares their faith to gold tested by fire. The hope doesn't remove the fire. It tells you what the fire is for. Then a line to the readers themselves: "Whom having not seen, you love." Peter had seen. They hadn't. He's writing to people who love someone they've never laid eyes on, and he tells them their joy is real anyway.
screen: `LIVELY MEANS LIVING.` · `HOPE, NOT A WEATHER FORECAST.` · `CAN'T PERISH, STAIN OR FADE.` · `WHOM HAVING NOT SEEN, YOU LOVE.` · then, large: `REGENERATED UNTO A LIVELY HOPE.`

segments.voice: Notice what you're carrying right now, the trial, the worry, whatever's heavy, and let it be there without fixing it. Underneath it, look for one hope bigger than this week, for someone you love, for the world, for yourself, and name it once, quietly. If you pray, hold it beside Peter's living hope, the resurrection; if not, let the hope sit beside the weight, both of them real.
Peter. The apostle who denied Christ three times by a fire, and years later opened his letter with a blessing: a living hope born of the resurrection. Today's word.
Your line: gold tested by fire. A hope that can't perish, stain or fade. See you tomorrow.

609.title: A royal priesthood (1 Peter 2:9)
609.hook: every baptized person shares Christ's priesthood (CCC 1268)
609.howItsDone: Catholics are anointed with chrism at baptism as sharers in Christ's role as priest, prophet and king, and some pray a Morning Offering each day, giving God their prayers, works, joys and sufferings; the Church distinguishes this common priesthood of all the baptized from the ordained priesthood.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Peter by the courtyard fire, and a living hope. Your line was gold tested by fire.

At a Catholic baptism, just after the water, the priest or deacon takes a small vessel of perfumed oil called chrism and anoints the crown of the baby's head. It's over in seconds, often under the sound of a crying baby. But the prayer said over that moment is startling. It says this child is now joined to Christ, who was anointed priest, prophet and king. A priest: a newborn who can't yet hold up her own head. The idea comes straight out of today's verse.
screen: `OIL ON A BABY'S HEAD.` → `PRIEST, PROPHET AND KING.` → `STRAIGHT OUT OF TODAY'S VERSE.`

segments.voice: Peter is writing to ordinary people: household servants, wives, converts living as strangers in their own towns. In the Douay-Rheims: "But you are a chosen generation, a kingly priesthood, a holy nation, a purchased people." The phrases are borrowed. At Mount Sinai, in the book of Exodus, God told Israel they would be a priestly kingdom and a holy nation. Peter gives those old titles to these scattered Christians, without taking them away from anyone. A few verses earlier he says they are living stones, built into a spiritual house, a holy priesthood, offering spiritual sacrifices. So what does a priest do? Stands between God and the world, and offers things up. The Catechism puts it plainly: every baptized person shares in the priesthood of Christ, the common priesthood of the faithful. It also teaches that the ordained priesthood is different, not just a higher level of the same thing, but a distinct gift for serving the whole people, especially at the altar. Both are real; neither replaces the other. On a Thursday, what does that look like? Paul gives a hint in Romans: "present your bodies a living sacrifice." The sacrifice is the day itself: the commute, the spreadsheet, the diaper, the hospital shift, the patience with a difficult relative, offered to God. Some Catholics begin each morning with a traditional prayer called the Morning Offering, giving God the prayers, works, joys and sufferings of the day ahead. A whole day, held up like bread at the altar.
screen: `OLD TITLES FROM SINAI.` · `LIVING STONES, SPIRITUAL SACRIFICES.` · `COMMON AND ORDAINED PRIESTHOOD.` · `THE DAY ITSELF, OFFERED UP.` · then, large: `A KINGLY PRIESTHOOD, A HOLY NATION.`

segments.voice: Walk through what's left of today: the work, the people, the chores, the thing you're dreading. Gather it all up in your hands, the good and the dull together, and lift it the way a priest lifts the bread at Mass. If you pray, offer it to God, perhaps with the Morning Offering; if not, hold the day up and look at it with care.
A royal priesthood. First Peter two nine: in Catholic teaching, every baptized person shares in Christ's priesthood, offering up their life. Today's word.
